questions.question: The lecture was so ________ that students who had come expecting to be challenged left with nothing more than a list of platitudes.

vapid
abstruse
incisive

questions.question: Though the critics were ________ in their praise of the debut, the author remained wary, having seen how quickly enthusiasm could curdle into contempt.
options: effusive
tepid
guarded
cursory

questions.question: The reformer's zeal was ________ by a stubborn pragmatism, so that for all his fiery speeches he never proposed a measure that could not pass.
options: stoked
amplified
tempered
ignited
questions.explanation: 'Tempered' means moderated, holding his zeal in check.

questions.question: While the new app was praised as innovative, its poor security turned out to be its ________, and users abandoned it within weeks.
options: golden goose
Trojan horse
Achilles' heel
lion's share

questions.question: The CEO's ________ optimism contrasted sharply with the ________ mood on the shop floor, where rumours of layoffs had made workers ________.

justified; buoyant; relaxed
feigned; jubilant; anxious
tepid; hopeful; assured

questions.question: Having ________ the evidence for years, the historian was ________ to find that the archive's newest document ________ her central thesis.

neglected; relieved; refuted
catalogued; gratified; undermined

questions.question: Rather than ________ the dispute, the court's ruling merely ________ it, leaving both parties at liberty to ________ the same arguments.
options: settle; postponed; repeat
worsen; resolved; abandon
ignore; escalated; forget
settle; ended; revive
questions.explanation: The ruling did not settle but postponed it, allowing parties to repeat arguments.

questions.question: The poet's late work, once dismissed as ________, is now admired for the very ________ that earlier critics ________.

obscure; simplicity; admired
trivial; depth; praised
obscure; density; deplored

questions.question: The explorer's account was ________ with exaggeration, but later expeditions ________ its broad outline while ________ many of its details.

riddled; confirmed; discarding
devoid; verified; embellishing
laden; refuted; preserving

questions.question: The report, along with its appendices, <u>were</u> submitted to the board on Friday.

are
being
was

that
as
than

has inspired
inspire
inspiring

questions.question: Examinations promise fairness by asking everyone the same questions. ____________________. A student who has never seen a multiple-choice format, or who reads the language of the paper as a second language, is being measured partly on something other than what the test claims to measure. Sameness of procedure, in short, is not the same as sameness of opportunity.
options: Many countries have therefore abolished written examinations in favour of continuous assessment in schools and colleges.
But identical questions do not guarantee that everyone meets them equally prepared.
Teachers generally prefer examinations because they are far easier and quicker to grade than projects or portfolios.
Examinations were first introduced in imperial China as a means of selecting civil servants for the state.
questions.explanation: Identical questions do not guarantee equal preparation.

questions.question: A translator is often called a traitor, but the proverb flatters the original. ____________________. Every language divides experience differently, and a word with no counterpart forces the translator to choose between fidelity to sense and fidelity to sound. Those choices are not betrayals; they are the work itself.
options: Many classic works are today available in dozens of languages thanks to the growth of modern publishing houses.
Machine translation has recently begun to rival human translators when handling ordinary everyday texts and documents.
Poetry is generally considered the hardest genre to translate because of its heavy dependence on rhyme and metre.
It assumes that a perfect version exists and that the translator has merely failed to deliver it.
questions.explanation: Assumes a perfect version exists that the translator failed to deliver.

questions.question: Cities that depend on a single industry enjoy remarkable prosperity while it lasts. ____________________. When the steel plant or the textile mill closes, the shops, schools and tax base that grew around it close with it, and the skills of the workforce are suddenly worth little. Diversification is dull in good years and invaluable in bad ones.
options: Governments in many countries have offered generous tax incentives to attract large manufacturers to small towns.
Such cities usually have better public transport and schools than those whose economies are more varied in character.
Steel and textiles were the two industries that contributed most to the industrial growth of the nineteenth century.
That prosperity, however, is a loan rather than a gift, repayable when the industry declines.
questions.explanation: Prosperity is a loan repayable when the industry declines.

questions.passage:
Karan Mehta (Host, Citywise Radio): Every monsoon, the same streets go under. Is this simply a rainfall problem?

Dr. Sunita Iyer (urban planner): Rainfall is the trigger, not the cause. Cities used to have lakes, marshes and open soil that absorbed water. We have paved over most of them, so the rain that once soaked in now runs off all at once and overwhelms drains designed for a smaller city.

Karan Mehta: So the answer is bigger drains?

Dr. Sunita Iyer: Only partly. Larger drains move the flood downstream and make it someone else's problem. The better approach is to slow the water down: restore wetlands, build permeable pavements, create retention ponds in parks.
questions.question: According to Dr. Iyer, the main cause of urban flooding is that
options: built-up cities have lost the soil and wetlands that once absorbed rainwater
monsoon rainfall has become far heavier in recent decades
existing drains are poorly maintained by city authorities
rivers and lakes are being drained to make way for farmland
questions.explanation: Cities lost soil and wetlands that absorbed rainwater.

questions.passage: Behavioural economists have popularised the idea of the 'nudge': a change in the way choices are presented that steers people toward better outcomes without forbidding anything. Enrolling employees in a pension scheme by default, with the freedom to opt out, is the standard illustration. Its defenders call this 'libertarian paternalism', a phrase meant to reassure both camps: nobody's options are removed, yet the architecture of choice leans in a welfare-enhancing direction. Critics respond that the reassurance is thin. Every choice must be presented somehow, so neutrality is not on offer; the real question is who selects the default and in whose interest. A government that sets the default is hardly an innocent bystander, and a firm that does so may be steering people toward its own margins rather than their welfare. There is also a subtler worry. A nudge works best when it bypasses deliberation, exploiting habit and inertia, and a policy that succeeds by circumventing reasoning sits uneasily with the ideal of citizens as reasoners. Defenders reply that people are already being nudged constantly, by supermarket layouts and app designs, and that the only choice is between nudges designed with care and nudges designed for profit. This is a fair point, but it proves less than it seems: that private actors manipulate us is an argument for restraining them, not a licence for the state to do likewise. What remains is a modest conclusion. Nudges are defensible where they are transparent, easily reversed and aligned with what people themselves would endorse on reflection, and suspect wherever they depend on being unnoticed.
questions.question: Which of the following best captures the author's conclusion about nudges?
options: Nudges are acceptable only when transparent, reversible and endorsable on reflection
Governments should abandon nudging altogether because any attempt to steer behaviour violates individual liberty and choice
Nudges are harmless, since people are already influenced by countless commercial pressures in everyday life
Default options are the most effective of all policy instruments for improving employee pension savings and welfare
questions.explanation: Nudges are defensible when transparent, reversible, and endorsable.

questions.passage: A map is usually taken to be a reduction of the world, a smaller and tidier copy of it. The cartographer's own training suggests the opposite: a map is an argument. Because the globe cannot be flattened without distortion, every projection chooses what to keep faithful, whether area, angle or distance, and what to sacrifice. The Mercator projection, devised for navigators who needed straight lines of constant compass bearing, enlarges regions near the poles; its later adoption in school atlases made Europe loom larger than Africa and encouraged, without anyone intending it, a quiet hierarchy of importance. Nor is the problem confined to geometry. A colonial survey that marked a river as a boundary and left a pastoral people's seasonal routes unrecorded did not merely describe a territory; it prepared the ground for who would be allowed to own it. Maps, in other words, do not follow power so much as help to make it. It would be a mistake, however, to conclude that all maps are propaganda and that the search for accuracy is naive. A railway diagram that abandons geography to make connections clear is not lying; it is answering the traveller's question. The sensible lesson is to ask of any map what it was drawn to help someone do, and what that purpose led its maker to leave out.
questions.question: The central claim of the passage is that
options: accurate maps are impossible to produce, so the pursuit of cartographic accuracy should be abandoned altogether by modern societies
colonial surveys were the main source of the distortion in the maps later used in schools around the world
maps embody choices and purposes, so they should be read as arguments, not neutral copies
the Mercator projection should be replaced in school atlases by projections that preserve the true size of every region
questions.explanation: Maps embody choices and purposes; they are arguments.

Because the globe cannot be flattened without distortion, every projection chooses what to keep faithful, whether area, angle or distance, and what to sacrifice. The Mercator projection, devised for navigators who needed straight lines of constant compass bearing, enlarges regions near the poles; its later adoption in school atlases made Europe loom larger than Africa and encouraged, without anyone intending it, a quiet hierarchy of importance. Nor is the problem confined to geometry. A colonial survey that marked a river as a boundary and left a pastoral people's seasonal routes unrecorded did not merely describe a territory; it prepared the ground for who would be allowed to own it. Maps, in other words, do not follow power so much as help to make it. It would be a mistake, however, to conclude that all maps are propaganda and that the search for accuracy is naive. A railway diagram that abandons geography to make connections clear is not lying; it is answering the traveller's question. The sensible lesson is to ask of any map what it was drawn to help someone do, and what that purpose led its maker to leave out.
questions.question: The railway diagram is mentioned in order to show that
options: maps intended for travellers are a special category exempt from the distortions found in other kinds of maps
geographic accuracy is irrelevant to every kind of map that is meant to be used in practical settings
the railway diagram proves that propaganda cannot occur in maps designed for practical everyday use
a map departing from geography can still be honest if it serves its purpose
questions.explanation: A map departing from geography can still be honest if it serves its purpose.

questions.question: Which of the following would the author most likely reject?
options: A map should be assessed in the light of the purpose it was originally drawn to serve its users
Because all projections distort, no map can be judged better than any other
Every choice about what a map includes necessarily involves something else being left out of it

questions.passage: The great nineteenth-century naturalists could, with some exaggeration, claim to know a whole science. Today a physicist may never read a paper outside a sub-subfield of a few hundred people. Specialisation is usually defended as the price of progress: knowledge has grown so vast that depth is possible only by narrowing. The defence is largely correct, yet it hides a cost that is easy to overlook because it does not appear in any single paper. Problems that matter rarely respect the boundaries of departments. Antibiotic resistance is at once a problem of microbiology, economics and hospital administration, and no specialist is trained to see all three at once. The usual response is the interdisciplinary team, but teams bring their own difficulties: members must spend so much effort translating between vocabularies that little remains for original thought, and credit tends to flow to the home discipline of the most senior member. A better remedy may be less glamorous. It is to ensure that a few researchers are rewarded for being broad rather than deep: people who read widely, connect findings across fields and ask questions no specialist would think to ask. Such people will rarely produce the sharpest result in any one area. Their value lies in noticing that two areas are secretly asking the same question, something the specialists, absorbed in their own corner, are least likely to see.
questions.question: Which of the following best states the main point of the passage?
options: Specialisation has been a mistake, and science should return to the nineteenth-century model of the universal naturalist
Interdisciplinary teams are the best solution to the problems created by increasing specialisation in modern science
Knowledge has grown too vast for any researcher to make a meaningful contribution outside a narrow subfield
Narrow specialisation carries a hidden cost, which rewarding some broad researchers could help offset
questions.explanation: Narrow specialisation carries a hidden cost offset by broad researchers.
